claim: Newly discovered lumbar vertebrae contribute to a near-complete lower back of Malapa Hominin 2 (MH2).
source: Newly discovered lumbar vertebrae contribute to a near-complete lower back of Malapa Hominin 2 (MH2), offering additional insights into posture and locomotion in Australopithecus sediba.
evidence: The abstract directly states this finding based on the fossil discoveries described in the manuscript.

claim: MH2 possessed a lower back consistent with lumbar lordosis.
source: We show that MH2 possessed a lower back consistent with lumbar lordosis and other adaptations to bipedalism, including an increase in the width of intervertebral articular facets from the upper to lower lumbar column ('pyramidal configuration').
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements and analyses of vertebral wedging angles presented in the manuscript.

claim: MH2 demonstrates an increase in the width of intervertebral articular facets from the upper to lower lumbar column ('pyramidal configuration').
source: We show that MH2 possessed a lower back consistent with lumbar lordosis and other adaptations to bipedalism, including an increase in the width of intervertebral articular facets from the upper to lower lumbar column ('pyramidal configuration').
evidence: This is supported by measurements and comparative analysis shown in Figure 6 and discussed in the results.

claim: MH2 was argued to demonstrate no appreciable lordosis ('hypolordosis') similar to Neandertals in some recent work.
source: These results contrast with some recent work on lordosis in fossil hominins, where MH2 was argued to demonstrate no appreciable lordosis ('hypolordosis') similar to Neandertals.
evidence: This references prior published work by Been et al., 2014, as cited elsewhere in the manuscript.

claim: MH2's nearly complete middle lumbar vertebra is human-like in overall shape.
source: Our three-dimensional geometric morphometric (3D GM) analyses show that MH2's nearly complete middle lumbar vertebra is human-like in overall shape but its vertebral body is somewhat intermediate in shape between modern humans and great apes.
evidence: This is supported by 3D geometric morphometric analyses presented in Figure 7.

claim: MH2's middle lumbar vertebral body is somewhat intermediate in shape between modern humans and great apes.
source: Our three-dimensional geometric morphometric (3D GM) analyses show that MH2's nearly complete middle lumbar vertebra is human-like in overall shape but its vertebral body is somewhat intermediate in shape between modern humans and great apes.
evidence: This is supported by 3D geometric morphometric analyses presented in Figure 7.

claim: MH2's middle lumbar vertebra bears long, cranially and ventrally oriented costal (transverse) processes.
source: Additionally, it bears long, cranially and ventrally oriented costal (transverse) processes, implying powerful trunk musculature.
evidence: This is based on direct observation and measurement of the fossil specimen U.W.88-233.

claim: Long, cranially and ventrally oriented costal processes imply powerful trunk musculature in A. sediba.
source: Additionally, it bears long, cranially and ventrally oriented costal (transverse) processes, implying powerful trunk musculature.
evidence: This is an inference based on functional morphology and biomechanical principles.

claim: A. sediba used its lower back in both bipedal and arboreal positional behaviors.
source: We interpret this combination of features to indicate that A. sediba used its lower back in both bipedal and arboreal positional behaviors, as previously suggested based on multiple lines of evidence from other parts of the skeleton and reconstructed paleobiology of A. sediba.
evidence: This interpretation is based on the combination of features observed in the current study and previous studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: Bipedal locomotion is thought to be one of the earliest and most extensive adaptations in the hominin lineage, potentially evolving initially 6–7 million years (Ma) ago.
source: Bipedal locomotion is thought to be one of the earliest and most extensive adaptations in the hominin lineage, potentially evolving initially 6–7 million years (Ma) ago.
evidence: This represents established scientific consensus in paleoanthropology.

claim: Human-like bipedalism evolved gradually.
source: Human-like bipedalism evolved gradually, however, and early hominins appear to have been facultative bipeds on the ground and competent climbers in the trees (Senut et al., 2001; White et al., 2015; Prang, 2019; Prang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Early hominins appear to have been facultative bipeds on the ground and competent climbers in the trees.
source: Human-like bipedalism evolved gradually, however, and early hominins appear to have been facultative bipeds on the ground and competent climbers in the trees (Senut et al., 2001; White et al., 2015; Prang, 2019; Prang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Australopithecus sediba is an early Pleistocene (~2 Ma) hominin from the site of Malapa, Gauteng province, South Africa.
source: Australopithecus sediba – an early Pleistocene (~2 Ma) hominin from the site of Malapa, Gauteng province, South Africa – has featured prominently in these discussions, as well as those concerning the origins of the genus Homo (Berger et al., 2010; Berger, 2012; Irish et al., 2013; Dembo et al., 2015; Kimbel and Rak, 2017; De Ruiter et al., 2018; Williams et al., 2018a; Du and Alemseged, 2019).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the geological age and location of the fossil, supported by citations.

claim: A. sediba possessed adaptations to arboreal locomotion.
source: Previous studies support the hypothesis that A. sediba possessed adaptations to arboreal locomotion and lacked traits reflecting a form of obligate terrestriality observed in later hominins (Schmid et al., 2013; Prang, 2015a; Prang, 2015b; Prang, 2016; Holliday et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A. sediba lacked traits reflecting a form of obligate terrestriality observed in later hominins.
source: Previous studies support the hypothesis that A. sediba possessed adaptations to arboreal locomotion and lacked traits reflecting a form of obligate terrestriality observed in later hominins (Schmid et al., 2013; Prang, 2015a; Prang, 2015b; Prang, 2016; Holliday et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: MH2 metacarpals are characterized by trabecular density most similar to orangutans, which suggests power grasping capabilities.
source: Malapa Hominin 2 (MH2) metacarpals are characterized by trabecular density most similar to orangutans, which suggests power grasping capabilities (Dunmore et al., 2020), and the MH2 ulna was estimated to reflect a high proportion of forelimb suspension in the locomotor repertoire of A. sediba (Rein et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dunmore et al., 2020.

claim: The MH2 ulna was estimated to reflect a high proportion of forelimb suspension in the locomotor repertoire of A. sediba.
source: Malapa Hominin 2 (MH2) metacarpals are characterized by trabecular density most similar to orangutans, which suggests power grasping capabilities (Dunmore et al., 2020), and the MH2 ulna was estimated to reflect a high proportion of forelimb suspension in the locomotor repertoire of A. sediba (Rein et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rein et al., 2017.

claim: A. sediba lacked a robust calcaneal tuber.
source: Evidence from the lower limb also suggests that A. sediba lacked a robust calcaneal tuber (Prang, 2015a) and a longitudinal arch (Prang, 2015b), both thought to be adaptations to obligate, human-like bipedalism, and demonstrates evidence for a mobile subtalar joint proposed to be adaptively significant for vertical climbing and other arboreal locomotor behaviors (Prang, 2016; DeSilva et al., 2013; Zipfel et al., 2011; DeSilva et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Prang, 2015a.

claim: A. sediba lacked a longitudinal arch.
source: Evidence from the lower limb also suggests that A. sediba lacked a robust calcaneal tuber (Prang, 2015a) and a longitudinal arch (Prang, 2015b), both thought to be adaptations to obligate, human-like bipedalism, and demonstrates evidence for a mobile subtalar joint proposed to be adaptively significant for vertical climbing and other arboreal locomotor behaviors (Prang, 2016; DeSilva et al., 2013; Zipfel et al., 2011; DeSilva et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Prang, 2015b.

claim: A robust calcaneal tuber and a longitudinal arch are thought to be adaptations to obligate, human-like bipedalism.
source: Evidence from the lower limb also suggests that A. sediba lacked a robust calcaneal tuber (Prang, 2015a) and a longitudinal arch (Prang, 2015b), both thought to be adaptations to obligate, human-like bipedalism, and demonstrates evidence for a mobile subtalar joint proposed to be adaptively significant for vertical climbing and other arboreal locomotor behaviors (Prang, 2016; DeSilva et al., 2013; Zipfel et al., 2011; DeSilva et al., 2018).
evidence: This represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: A. sediba demonstrates evidence for a mobile subtalar joint proposed to be adaptively significant for vertical climbing and other arboreal locomotor behaviors.
source: Evidence from the lower limb also suggests that A. sediba lacked a robust calcaneal tuber (Prang, 2015a) and a longitudinal arch (Prang, 2015b), both thought to be adaptations to obligate, human-like bipedalism, and demonstrates evidence for a mobile subtalar joint proposed to be adaptively significant for vertical climbing and other arboreal locomotor behaviors (Prang, 2016; DeSilva et al., 2013; Zipfel et al., 2011; DeSilva et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The upper thorax of A. sediba suggests shoulder and arm elevation indicative of arboreal positional behaviors requiring overhead arm positions.
source: The upper thorax (Schmid et al., 2013), scapula (Churchill et al., 2013; Churchill et al., 2018), and cervical vertebrae (Meyer et al., 2017) of A. sediba suggest shoulder and arm elevation indicative of arboreal positional behaviors requiring overhead arm positions, and the limb joint size proportions are ape-like (Prabhat et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The scapula of A. sediba suggests shoulder and arm elevation indicative of arboreal positional behaviors requiring overhead arm positions.
source: The upper thorax (Schmid et al., 2013), scapula (Churchill et al., 2013; Churchill et al., 2018), and cervical vertebrae (Meyer et al., 2017) of A. sediba suggest shoulder and arm elevation indicative of arboreal positional behaviors requiring overhead arm positions, and the limb joint size proportions are ape-like (Prabhat et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The cervical vertebrae of A. sediba suggest shoulder and arm elevation indicative of arboreal positional behaviors requiring overhead arm positions.
source: The upper thorax (Schmid et al., 2013), scapula (Churchill et al., 2013; Churchill et al., 2018), and cervical vertebrae (Meyer et al., 2017) of A. sediba suggest shoulder and arm elevation indicative of arboreal positional behaviors requiring overhead arm positions, and the limb joint size proportions are ape-like (Prabhat et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Meyer et al., 2017.

claim: The limb joint size proportions of A. sediba are ape-like.
source: The upper thorax (Schmid et al., 2013), scapula (Churchill et al., 2013; Churchill et al., 2018), and cervical vertebrae (Meyer et al., 2017) of A. sediba suggest shoulder and arm elevation indicative of arboreal positional behaviors requiring overhead arm positions, and the limb joint size proportions are ape-like (Prabhat et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Prabhat et al., 2021.

claim: Analysis of dental calculus from Malapa Hominin 1 (MH1) indicates that this individual's diet was high in C3 plants like fruit and leaves, similar to savannah chimpanzees and Ardipithecus ramidus.
source: Furthermore, analysis of dental calculus from Malapa Hominin 1 (MH1) indicates that this individual's diet was high in C3 plants like fruit and leaves, similar to savannah chimpanzees and Ardipithecus ramidus (Henry et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Henry et al., 2012.

claim: The knee and ankle of A. sediba possess human-like adaptations to bipedalism.
source: The knee and ankle possess human-like adaptations to bipedalism, demonstrating a valgus angle of the femur and a human-like ankle joint (Zipfel et al., 2011; DeSilva et al., 2013; DeSilva et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A. sediba demonstrates a valgus angle of the femur.
source: The knee and ankle possess human-like adaptations to bipedalism, demonstrating a valgus angle of the femur and a human-like ankle joint (Zipfel et al., 2011; DeSilva et al., 2013; DeSilva et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A. sediba demonstrates a human-like ankle joint.
source: The knee and ankle possess human-like adaptations to bipedalism, demonstrating a valgus angle of the femur and a human-like ankle joint (Zipfel et al., 2011; DeSilva et al., 2013; DeSilva et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Evidence for strong dorsal (lordotic) wedging of the two lower lumbar vertebrae suggests the presence of a lordotic (ventrally convex) lower back in A. sediba.
source: Evidence for strong dorsal (lordotic) wedging of the two lower lumbar vertebrae suggests the presence of a lordotic (ventrally convex) lower back (Williams et al., 2013; Williams et al., 2018b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies by the authors.

claim: A study of the MH2 pelvis reconstruction suggests that A. sediba was characterized by a small lordosis angle estimated from calculated pelvic incidence.
source: However, the initial recovery of just the last two lumbar vertebrae of MH2 limited interpretations of spinal curvature, and a study of the MH2 pelvis reconstruction (Kibii et al., 2011) suggests that A. sediba was characterized by a small lordosis angle estimated from calculated pelvic incidence (Been et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kibii et al., 2011 and Been et al., 2014.

claim: A separate pelvis reconstruction of MH2 produces a pelvic incidence angle more in line with other hominins.
source: A separate pelvis reconstruction of MH2 produces a pelvic incidence angle more in line with other hominins (Tardieu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tardieu et al., 2017.

claim: The presence of a long, mobile lower back and a Homo-like lower thorax morphology indicating the presence of a waist suggest bipedal adaptations in A. sediba.
source: The presence of a long, mobile lower back and a Homo-like lower thorax morphology indicating the presence of a waist further suggest bipedal adaptations in A. sediba (Schmid et al., 2013; Williams et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Portions of four lumbar vertebrae were discovered from two ex situ breccia blocks that were excavated from an early 20th century mining road and dump at Malapa.
source: Here, we report the discovery of portions of four lumbar vertebrae from two ex situ breccia blocks that were excavated from an early 20th century mining road and dump at Malapa.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the discovery context.

claim: The former mining road is represented by a trackway located in the northern section of the site approximately 2 m north of the main pit that yielded the original A. sediba finds.
source: The former mining road is represented by a trackway located in the northern section of the site approximately 2 m north of the main pit that yielded the original A. sediba finds (Dirks et al., 2010; Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 1 and citation to Dirks et al., 2010.

claim: Specimens U.W.88–232, −233,–234, and –281 were recovered in 2015 from the upper section of layer 2 (at a depth of 10 cm).
source: Specimens U.W.88–232, −233,–234, and –281 were recovered in 2015 from the upper section of layer 2 (at a depth of 10 cm) and formed part of the foundation layer of the mining road.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the discovery context.

claim: The geological evidence suggests that the material used for the construction of the miner's road was sourced on-site, and most probably originated from the northern section of the main pit.
source: Therefore, the geological evidence suggests that the material used for the construction of the miner's road was sourced on-site, and most probably originated from the northern section of the main pit.
evidence: This is an inference based on geological analysis of the breccia composition.

claim: The newly discovered vertebrae (second and third lumbar) are preserved in articulation with each other.
source: The newly discovered vertebrae (second and third lumbar) are preserved in articulation with each other (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and refit at multiple contacts with the previously known penultimate (fourth) lumbar vertebra (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figures 2 and 3.

claim: The new vertebrae refit at multiple contacts with the previously known penultimate (fourth) lumbar vertebra.
source: The newly discovered vertebrae (second and third lumbar) are preserved in articulation with each other (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and refit at multiple contacts with the previously known penultimate (fourth) lumbar vertebra (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 3.

claim: The new and previously known vertebral elements form a continuous series from the antepenultimate thoracic vertebra through the fifth sacral element, with only the first lumbar vertebra missing major components of morphology.
source: Together, the new and previously known (Williams et al., 2013; Williams et al., 2018b) vertebral elements form a continuous series from the antepenultimate thoracic vertebra through the fifth sacral element, with only the first lumbar vertebra missing major components of morphology (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and citations to previous work.

claim: U.W.88–280 is a partial, superior portion of a vertebral body concealed in the matrix of a previously known block containing lower thoracic vertebrae.
source: U.W.88–280: This is a partial, superior portion of a vertebral body concealed in the matrix of a previously known block containing lower thoracic vertebrae (U.W.88–114, U.W.88–43, and U.W.88–44, antepenultimate, penultimate, and ultimate thoracic vertebrae, respectively, of MH2) (Williams et al., 2018b).
evidence: This is a descriptive statement about the fossil specimen.

claim: U.W.88–280 was revealed in the segmentation of micro-CT data.
source: U.W.88–280 was revealed in the segmentation of micro-CT (hereafter, µCT) data.
evidence: This describes the method by which the fossil was identified.

claim: U.W.88–280 represents part of the first lumbar vertebra of MH2.
source: We identify this as part (along with U.W.88–281) of the first lumbar vertebra of MH2 based on its position below the vertebral body of what is almost certainly the last thoracic vertebra (U.W.88–44) (Williams et al., 2018b; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This identification is based on anatomical position and comparison with previously known elements.

claim: U.W.88–281 is the partial neural arch of a post-transitional, upper lumbar vertebra concealed in matrix above the subjacent lumbar vertebra (U.W.88–232).
source: U.W.88–281: This is the partial neural arch of a post-transitional, upper lumbar vertebra concealed in matrix above the subjacent lumbar vertebra (U.W.88–232).
evidence: This is a descriptive statement about the fossil specimen.

claim: U.W.88–281 was revealed through the segmentation of µCT data.
source: It was revealed through the segmentation of µCT data.
evidence: This describes the method by which the fossil was identified.

claim: U.W.88–281 is fixed in partial articulation with the subjacent second lumbar vertebra (L2), U.W.88–232.
source: U.W.88–281 is fixed in partial articulation with the subjacent second lumbar vertebra (L2), U.W.88–232.
evidence: This is a descriptive statement about the fossil specimen's position.

claim: U.W.88–232 is the L2 and remains in articulation with the third lumbar vertebra (L3), U.W.88–233.
source: U.W.88–232: This vertebra is the L2 and remains in articulation with the third lumbar vertebra (L3), U.W.88–233, held together with matrix.
evidence: This is a descriptive statement about the fossil specimen.

claim: U.W.88–232 is mostly complete, missing the cranial portions of its superior articular processes and distal portions of its costal (transverse) processes.
source: U.W.88–232 is mostly complete, missing the cranial portions of its superior articular processes and distal portions of its costal (transverse) processes.
evidence: This is a descriptive statement about the fossil specimen's preservation.

claim: U.W.88–233 is the L3 and the most complete vertebra in the lumbar series.
source: U.W.88–233: This is the L3 and the most complete vertebra in the lumbar series, although some aspects of the neural arch are distorted, broken, and displaced.
evidence: This is a descriptive statement about the fossil specimen.

claim: U.W.88–233 is essentially complete.
source: U.W.88–233 is essentially complete; however, like U.W.88–232, the neural arch is crushed from the dorsal direction, with breaks and displacement across the right pars interarticularis and the right costal process at its base, with additional buckling around the latter near the base of the of the right superior articular process, resulting in a crushing of the vertebral foramen.
evidence: This is a descriptive statement about the fossil specimen's preservation.

claim: U.W.88–234 is a partial neural arch of the previously known penultimate lumbar vertebra (L4).
source: U.W.88–234: This is a partial neural arch of the previously known penultimate lumbar vertebra (L4) (U.W.88-127/153).
evidence: This is a descriptive statement about the fossil specimen.

claim: U.W.88–234 refits in two places with the previously known L4.
source: U.W.88–234 refits in two places with the previously known L4: its partial pedicle with the vertebral body (U.W.88–127) and its spinous process with the inferior base of the spinous process and inferior articular processes (U.W.88–153) (Figures 2–3).
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figures 2-3.

claim: MH2 possesses the greatest (i.e., most negative) combined wedging value of any adult early hominin (–6.8°).
source: MH2 possesses the greatest (i.e., most negative) combined wedging value of any adult early hominin (–6.8°).
evidence: This is based on measurements and comparative analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: All fossil hominins fall within the 95% prediction intervals of modern humans in combined L2-L5 wedging.
source: Although all fossil hominins fall within the 95% prediction intervals of modern humans, only MH2 falls outside the 95% prediction intervals of great apes in combined L2-L5 wedging (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in Figure 5.

claim: Only MH2 falls outside the 95% prediction intervals of great apes in combined L2-L5 wedging.
source: Although all fossil hominins fall within the 95% prediction intervals of modern humans, only MH2 falls outside the 95% prediction intervals of great apes in combined L2-L5 wedging (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in Figure 5.

claim: MH2's vertebrae transition from ventral (kyphotic) to dorsal (lordotic) wedging between the L3 and L4 levels.
source: Patterns of change across lumbar levels demonstrate that MH2's vertebrae transition from ventral (kyphotic) to dorsal (lordotic) wedging between the L3 and L4 levels; however, all adult fossil hominins fall within the 95% prediction intervals of modern humans (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on measurements and analysis presented in Figure 5 and supplements.

claim: The last lumbar vertebra of MH2 is strongly dorsally wedged like that of the Kebara 2 Neandertal and the juvenile specimen KNM-WT 15000.
source: As shown previously (Williams et al., 2013), the last lumbar vertebra of MH2 is strongly dorsally wedged like that of the Kebara 2 Neandertal and the juvenile specimen KNM-WT 15000, whereas other fossil hominins do not demonstrate this pattern.
evidence: This is based on comparative measurements and previous work cited.

claim: The pattern of lumbar wedging angles observed in MH2 and its combined L2-L5 wedging fall within the modern human 95% PIs and outside those of great apes.
source: Although vertebral wedging is characterized by high levels of variation within groups, especially in combined L2-L5 wedging (Figure 5, Table 2), the pattern of lumbar wedging angles observed in MH2 (i.e., transition from penultimate to ultimate lumbar level) and its combined L2-L5 wedging fall within the modern human 95% PIs and outside those of great apes (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in Figure 5 and supplements.

claim: Humans are characterized by a pyramidal configuration of the articular facets such that they increase in transverse width progressively down the lumbar column.
source: Humans are characterized by a pyramidal configuration of the articular facets such that they increase in transverse width progressively down the lumbar column (i.e., from cranial to caudal) (Latimer and Ward, 1993; Ward and Latimer, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Australopithecus africanus (Sts 14 and StW 431; average = 1.42) and A. sediba (1.43) fall at the low end of the range of modern human variation in the lumbar inter-articular facet index.
source: Using an index of the last lumbar-sacrum inter-articular maximum distance relative to that of lumbar vertebrae three levels higher (L2-L3 in hominins, L1-L2 in chimpanzees and gorillas), we show that Australopithecus africanus (Sts 14 and StW 431; average = 1.42) and A. sediba (1.43) fall at the low end of the range of modern human variation in this trait (Figure 6).
evidence: This is based on measurements and comparative analysis presented in Figure 6.

claim: Homo erectus and Neandertals fall well within the range of modern human variation in the lumbar inter-articular facet index.
source: Homo erectus and Neandertals fall well within the range of modern human variation.
evidence: This is based on comparative analysis of the lumbar inter-articular facet index.

claim: The presence of a pyramidal configuration of the lumbar articular facets is present in MH2.
source: The presence of a pyramidal configuration of the lumbar articular facets is therefore present in MH2, supporting our hypothesis that A. sediba was adapted to a human-like configuration of the neural arch.
evidence: This is based on measurements and comparative analysis.

claim: A. sediba falls within or near the human distribution on the first three principal components (PC1–3) in 3D GM analysis of middle lumbar vertebra shape.
source: The results of our principal components analysis (PCA) on Procrustes-aligned shape coordinates reveal that A. sediba falls within or near the human distribution on the first three principal components (PC1–3) (Figure 7).
evidence: This is supported by the 3D GM analysis presented in Figure 7.

claim: PC1 explains 31% of the variance in the middle lumbar vertebra shape dataset.
source: PC1 explains 31% of the variance in the dataset, and along it hominins are characterized by more sagittally oriented and concave superior articular facets (SAF), more dorsally oriented costal processes, a dorsoventrally shorter and cranially oriented spinous process, craniocaudally shorter, dorsoventrally longer vertebral body, and more caudally positioned SAF and IAF relative to the vertebral body compared to great apes.
evidence: This is based on the PCA results.

claim: Along PC1, hominins are characterized by more sagittally oriented and concave superior articular facets, more dorsally oriented costal processes, a dorsoventrally shorter and cranially oriented spinous process, craniocaudally shorter, dorsoventrally longer vertebral body, and more caudally positioned SAF and IAF relative to the vertebral body compared to great apes.
source: PC1 explains 31% of the variance in the dataset, and along it hominins are characterized by more sagittally oriented and concave superior articular facets (SAF), more dorsally oriented costal processes, a dorsoventrally shorter and cranially oriented spinous process, craniocaudally shorter, dorsoventrally longer vertebral body, and more caudally positioned SAF and IAF relative to the vertebral body compared to great apes.
evidence: This is based on the PCA results and interpretation of shape variation.

claim: PC2 explains 13% of the variance in middle lumbar vertebra shape and contrasts long spinous processes and relatively neutrally wedged vertebral bodies of hominins and African apes with the shorter spinous processes and strongly ventrally wedged vertebral bodies of orangutans.
source: PC2 explains 13% of the variance and contrasts long spinous processes and relatively neutrally wedged (~0° ± 1°) vertebral bodies of hominins and African apes with the shorter spinous processes and strongly ventrally wedged vertebral bodies of orangutans.
evidence: This is based on the PCA results.

claim: PC3 explains 8% of the variance in middle lumbar vertebra shape and largely contrasts dorsoventrally longer vertebral bodies with caudally oriented spinous processes in gorillas with dorsoventrally shorter vertebral bodies and less caudally oriented spinous processes in chimpanzees and orangutans.
source: PC3 explains 8% of the variance and largely contrasts dorsoventrally longer vertebral bodies with caudally oriented spinous processes in gorillas with dorsoventrally shorter vertebral bodies and less caudally oriented spinous processes in chimpanzees and orangutans; hominins fall intermediate between these groups.
evidence: This is based on the PCA results.

claim: PC4 explains 5% of the variance in middle lumbar vertebra shape and contrasts A. sediba and A. africanus with both humans and great apes.
source: PC4 explains 5% of the variance, and contrasts A. sediba and A. africanus with both humans and great apes.
evidence: This is based on the PCA results.

claim: Sts 14 and especially U.W.88–233 are characterized by longer, taller, more cranially oriented costal processes that do not taper distally and more sagittally oriented articular facets.
source: Sts 14 and especially U.W.88–233 are characterized by longer, taller, more cranially oriented costal processes that do not taper distally and more sagittally oriented (as opposed to more coronally oriented) articular facets (Figure 7, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on the 3D GM analysis and visual inspection of the fossils.

claim: U.W.88–233 is most similar to Sts 14 among fossil and extant specimens in Procrustes distance.
source: These analyses demonstrate that U.W.88–233 is most similar to Sts 14 among fossil and extant specimens included.
evidence: This is based on Procrustes distance analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Centroid size has a significant effect on lumbar shape (F = 9.83; p < 0.001).
source: The results show significant effects of centroid size (F = 9.83; p < 0.001), genus (with hominins pooled; F = 27.7; p < 0.001), and an interaction between genus and centroid size (F = 1.48; p = 0.01), implying unique shape allometries within genera (Table 4).
evidence: This is based on Procrustes ANOVA results presented in Table 4.

claim: Genus has a significant effect on lumbar shape (F = 27.7; p < 0.001).
source: The results show significant effects of centroid size (F = 9.83; p < 0.001), genus (with hominins pooled; F = 27.7; p < 0.001), and an interaction between genus and centroid size (F = 1.48; p = 0.01), implying unique shape allometries within genera (Table 4).
evidence: This is based on Procrustes ANOVA results presented in Table 4.

claim: There is a significant interaction between genus and centroid size (F = 1.48; p = 0.01), implying unique shape allometries within genera.
source: The results show significant effects of centroid size (F = 9.83; p < 0.001), genus (with hominins pooled; F = 27.7; p < 0.001), and an interaction between genus and centroid size (F = 1.48; p = 0.01), implying unique shape allometries within genera (Table 4).
evidence: This is based on Procrustes ANOVA results and represents an inference about shape allometry.

claim: Larger centroid sizes are associated with dorsoventrally longer and more caudally projecting spinous processes, more cranially oriented and less sagittally oriented costal processes, and less caudally projecting IAF.
source: In general, larger centroid sizes are associated with 3D shape changes including dorsoventrally longer and more caudally projecting spinous processes, more cranially oriented and less sagittally oriented costal processes, and less caudally projecting IAF.
evidence: This is based on multivariate regression analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: The cranially oriented costal processes of U.W.88–233 (and Sts 14) appear not to be explained by centroid size.
source: Importantly, however, the cranially oriented costal processes of U.W.88–233 (and Sts 14) appear not to be explained by centroid size given its relatively small size and overlap with Pan in standardized shape scores (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is based on the allometry analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: MH2 was probably neither hypolordotic nor hyperlordotic and produces a combined wedging angles value more similar to modern humans than great apes.
source: Therefore, it seems likely that MH2 and possibly the juvenile H. erectus individual KNM-WT 15000 demonstrate strong dorsal wedging at the last lumbar level for different reasons than Kebara 2. It was suggested previously that the morphology of the MH2 last lumbar is part of a kinematic chain linked to hyperpronation of the foot (DeSilva et al., 2013; Williams et al., 2013). With the absence of soft tissue contributions to the kinematic chain (i.e., intervertebral discs), formal biomechanical testing is beyond the scope of the current paper; however, our results suggest that MH2 was probably neither hypolordotic nor hyperlordotic and produces a combined wedging angles value more similar to modern humans than great apes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the wedging angle data and comparison with extant taxa.

claim: Modern humans are characterized by a pyramidal configuration of the lumbar inter-articular facet joints such that the upper lumbar articular facet joints are transversely more narrowly spaced than those of the lower lumbar vertebrae.
source: Modern humans are characterized by a pyramidal configuration of the lumbar inter-articular facet joints such that the upper lumbar articular facet joints (and associated laminae) are transversely more narrowly spaced than those of the lower lumbar vertebrae and especially compared to the lumbosacral inter-articular facet joints (Latimer and Ward, 1993; Sanders, 1998; Ward and Latimer, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Progressive widening of inter-articular facets facilitates the adoption of lordotic posture during ontogeny and allows for the imbrication of the IAF of a superjacent vertebra onto the laminae of the subjacent vertebra during hyperextension of the lower back.
source: Together with vertebral body and intervertebral disc wedging, this progressive widening facilitates the adoption of lordotic posture during ontogeny and allows for the imbrication of the IAF of a superjacent vertebra onto the laminae of the subjacent vertebra during hyperextension of the lower back (Latimer and Ward, 1993; Williams et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research and represents functional interpretation.

claim: Known fossil hominin lumbar vertebrae bear 'imbrication pockets', mechanically induced fossae positioned just caudal to the SAF on the lamina, providing direct evidence for lumbar hyperextension and lordosis.
source: Like modern humans, known fossil hominin lumbar vertebrae bear 'imbrication pockets', mechanically induced fossae positioned just caudal to the SAF on the lamina (Latimer and Ward, 1993; Williams et al., 2013), providing direct evidence for lumbar hyperextension and lordosis.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Inadequate spacing of lower lumbar inter-articular facets in modern humans can result in spondylolysis, fracture of the pars interarticularis, and potential separation of the affected vertebra's spinous process and inferior articular processes.
source: Inadequate spacing of lower lumbar inter-articular facets in modern humans can result in spondylolysis, fracture of the pars interarticularis, and potential separation of the affected vertebra's spinous process and inferior articular processes (Ward and Latimer, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research and represents clinical/anatomical knowledge.

claim: Russo and Shapiro, 2013, demonstrated that measures for changes in both interfacet distance and laminar width in Oreopithecus fall within ranges of extant apes and outside those of humans.
source: Although a human-like pattern of interfacet distance was once claimed for the European late Miocene ape Oreopithecus (Köhler and Moya-Sola, 1997), Russo and Shapiro, 2013, demonstrated that measures for changes in both interfacet distance and laminar width in this extinct ape fall within ranges of extant apes (and other suspensory mammals) and outside those of humans.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Russo and Shapiro, 2013.

claim: Latimer and Ward, 1993, documented the presence of a pyramidal configuration in H. erectus.
source: Among hominins, Latimer and Ward, 1993, documented the presence of a pyramidal configuration in H. erectus.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Latimer and Ward, 1993.

claim: A pyramidal configuration has been demonstrated qualitatively in A. afarensis and A. africanus.
source: It has also been demonstrated qualitatively in A. afarensis and A. africanus (Robinson, 1972; Lovejoy, 2005), and its presence in A. sediba could be inferred previously based on the articulated penultimate and ultimate lumbar vertebrae and sacrum of MH2 (Williams et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: MH2 and other Australopithecus specimens fall at the low end of modern human variation and differ from great apes in having significantly wider inter-articular facets at the lumbosacral junction than higher in the lumbar column.
source: Here, we show that MH2 and other Australopithecus specimens fall at the low end of modern human variation and differ from great apes in having significantly wider inter-articular facets at the lumbosacral junction than higher in the lumbar column (Figure 6).
evidence: This is based on measurements and comparative analysis presented in Figure 6.

claim: The overall morphologies of lumbar vertebrae are informative with regard to locomotion and posture in primates.
source: The overall morphologies of lumbar vertebrae are informative with regard to locomotion and posture in primates (Slijper, 1946; Shapiro, 1993b; Sanders and Bodenbender, 1994; Granatosky et al., 2014; Williams and Russo, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research and represents established knowledge.

claim: Hominoids are characterized by derived vertebral morphologies related to orthogrady and antipronograde positional behaviors.
source: Hominoids are characterized by derived vertebral morphologies related to orthogrady and antipronograde positional behaviors, and early hominins have been found to largely resemble modern humans in lumbar vertebra shape, with some retained primitive morphologies (Robinson, 1972; Schmid, 1991; Shapiro, 1993a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research and represents established knowledge.

claim: Early hominins have been found to largely resemble modern humans in lumbar vertebra shape, with some retained primitive morphologies.
source: Hominoids are characterized by derived vertebral morphologies related to orthogrady and antipronograde positional behaviors, and early hominins have been found to largely resemble modern humans in lumbar vertebra shape, with some retained primitive morphologies (Robinson, 1972; Schmid, 1991; Shapiro, 1993a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Long costal processes give the psoas major and quadratus lumborum muscles an effective leverage in acting on the vertebral column, increasing their moment arms and torque generation capabilities.
source: Long costal processes give the psoas major and quadratus lumborum muscles an effective leverage in acting on the vertebral column, increasing their moment arms and torque generation capabilities to assist the erector spinae in lateral flexion of the spine, back extension, and stabilizing the trunk during upright posture and bipedalism and ape-like vertical climbing (Robinson, 1972; Waters and Morris, 1972; Schmid, 1991; Sanders, 1998; Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on biomechanical principles and supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Psoas major acts with iliacus as a powerful flexor of the thigh and trunk.
source: Psoas major acts with iliacus as a powerful flexor of the thigh and trunk, while quadratus lumborum is a trunk extensor and a lateral flexor of the vertebral column and pelvis unilaterally (Robinson, 1972; Drake et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations and represents anatomical knowledge.

claim: Quadratus lumborum is a trunk extensor and a lateral flexor of the vertebral column and pelvis unilaterally.
source: Psoas major acts with iliacus as a powerful flexor of the thigh and trunk, while quadratus lumborum is a trunk extensor and a lateral flexor of the vertebral column and pelvis unilaterally (Robinson, 1972; Drake et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations and represents anatomical knowledge.

claim: The lumbar vertebral morphology of A. sediba is that of a biped equipped with especially powerful trunk musculature for stabilizing the hip and back during walking and/or vertical climbing.
source: The lumbar vertebral morphology of A. sediba, therefore, is that of a biped equipped with especially powerful trunk musculature for stabilizing the hip and back during walking and/or vertical climbing.
evidence: This is an inference based on the morphological features observed and functional anatomy.

claim: The new fossils reinforce conclusions that MH2 has a lower back as that of an upright biped equipped with powerful trunk musculature potentially used in both terrestrial and arboreal locomotion.
source: The new fossils here reinforce these conclusions, signaling a lower back in MH2 as that of an upright biped equipped with powerful trunk musculature potentially used in both terrestrial and arboreal locomotion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combination of features observed in the new fossils and previous studies.

claim: Wedging of articulated vertebrae contribute to the multiple sagittal curvatures of the human spine.
source: Wedging of articulated vertebrae contribute to the multiple sagittal curvatures of the human spine, with dorsal wedging of lower lumbar vertebrae contributing to a ventrally convex curvature of the lumbar spine (lumbar lordosis).
evidence: This represents established anatomical knowledge.

claim: Dorsal wedging of lower lumbar vertebrae contributes to a ventrally convex curvature of the lumbar spine (lumbar lordosis).
source: Wedging of articulated vertebrae contribute to the multiple sagittal curvatures of the human spine, with dorsal wedging of lower lumbar vertebrae contributing to a ventrally convex curvature of the lumbar spine (lumbar lordosis).
evidence: This represents established anatomical knowledge.

claim: The sinusoidal configuration of the human spine passively balances the upper body over the pelvis and allows for the unique system of weight bearing and force transmission found in members of the human lineage.
source: This sinusoidal configuration passively balances the upper body over the pelvis and allows for the unique system of weight bearing and force transmission found in members of the human lineage (Davis, 1961; Robinson, 1972; Pal and Routal, 1987; Latimer and Ward, 1993; Shapiro, 1993a; Lovejoy, 2005; Whitcome et al., 2007; Masharawi et al., 2010; Been et al., 2014; Tardieu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations and represents established knowledge.
